stops.name: Saguntum, the siege begins
stops.campa: Saguntum sits on its long rock above the sea, friend of Rome south of the Ebro: the tripwire both cities have laid and both pretend not to see. Hannibal invests it in the spring. The Saguntines hurl the falarica, the great fire-javelin with its burning tow, and fight like a city that expects the world to come save it. Under the wall a javelin passes through Hannibal's thigh; the siege slackens while he lies bleeding, then closes again harder. Rome sends envoys; he does not receive them. The world does not come.

stops.name: Saguntum, the fall in the eighth month
stops.campa: In the eighth month the towers come down and the town is taken street by street. The leading men heap their gold and silver into a fire in the forum and throw themselves after it; the rest die armed or under the roofs. The plunder pays an army and buys half of Carthage's council. Across the sea a Roman, Fabius, will soon stand in that council holding two folds of his toga, peace here, war here, and Carthage will answer: give us whichever you please. The fold falls open. It is war.

stops.name: Gades, the vows paid to Melqart
stops.campa: Before the great war he goes down to Gades, to the temple at the world's edge where he stood as a boy, and discharges his old vows to Melqart and binds himself with new ones. The god of his fathers, the wandering Herakles of Tyre, is made patron of the march: as Melqart once drove the cattle of the sun through these same lands to Italy, so the army will walk the god's own road. He returns to New Carthage with the god at his shoulder.

stops.name: New Carthage, the muster of the nations
stops.campa: Spring opens the roads and the army stands on the parade grounds of Qart Hadasht: ninety thousand foot, twelve thousand horse, thirty-seven elephants, Libyans, Iberians, Numidians, slingers of the Balearics. He sends Iberian troops home to Africa and African troops to Iberia, each a hostage for the other's country; leaves his brother Hasdrubal the sea and the province; dismisses the doubtful to their villages with thanks, keeping only the willing. Then the trumpets, and the column uncoils toward the Ebro, and nothing about the world will be the same.

stops.name: The Ebro crossing, the dream of the serpent
stops.campa: The army crosses the Ebro in three columns, and that night the gods come for their general. In his sleep a youth of more than mortal beauty says he is sent by Jupiter to guide him into Italy: follow, and do not look back. Hannibal follows; then, as men must, he looks. Behind him a serpent of monstrous bulk drags itself forward, and forests and hillsides crash down before it, and a storm-cloud walks behind with thunder. What is this? he asks. The devastation of Italy, the youth answers. Go forward, and ask nothing more.

stops.name: The Pyrenees, the Col de Pertús
stops.campa: The tribes between Ebro and mountains are broken in weeks and Hanno is left to hold the new country. At the passes three thousand Carpetani, frightened less by the enemy than by the length of the road, turn for home; Hannibal, reading the army's heart, sends seven thousand more after them with his blessing, as if he had dismissed them himself. Fifty thousand foot and nine thousand horse, willing, all of them, cross the Pyrenees light. Fear stays behind on the Spanish side.

stops.name: Ruscino, the parley with the Gauls
stops.campa: The Gallic chiefs gather in arms at Ruscino, minded to bar the road. Hannibal invites them into his own camp instead: come to me, or I will come to you, and receives them with gifts and gold and the plain statement that he is a guest in Gaul, not an enemy, and will not draw a sword north of the mountains unless one is drawn on him. The chiefs go home rich and persuaded. The army passes through their country buying its bread, a wonder the Gauls speak of for a generation.

stops.name: The Rhone, the elephants on the rafts
stops.campa: The Volcae mass on the far bank; Hanno son of Bomilcar swims a division across upstream on skins and fires their camp at the signal-smoke, and the crossing is won. Then the elephants: great piers of lashed rafts are run out from the bank, floored with earth so the beasts believe they walk on land; the females lead; when the towed sections swing into the current the elephants panic, and some plunge in and drown their mahouts, but the beasts themselves, trunks raised above the water, walk the riverbed and come up on the Italian side. The river is beaten. Scipio's scouts arrive to find only cold fires.

stops.name: The Island, the kingmaker at the Isère
stops.campa: Four days up the Rhone lies the Island, rich land in the fork of the rivers, where two brothers are at war for the kingship of the Allobroges. Hannibal, arriving with an army, is asked to judge between them, and crowns the elder, Brancus. The new king pays for his crown royally: grain, new boots for the whole army, wool cloaks against the mountains, weapons reissued, and an escort of his warriors to cover the rear. The Carthaginian walks toward the Alps shod and clothed by a king he made in an afternoon.

stops.name: The Gates of the Alps, the first ambush
stops.campa: Where the escort turns back, the mountain Allobroges take up the tolls. They hold the heights above the one track, but only by day, going home to their town at dusk; Hannibal learns it from his Gallic scouts, lights his campfires as if bedded down, and takes the abandoned heights in the dark. At dawn the tribesmen attack anyway, and the column pays: horses hit by javelins scream and fall outward off the track, dragging their loads into the gorge. Hannibal comes down from his crag like a landslide himself, sweeps the attackers off, storms their white-walled town, and feeds the army three days from its stores.

stops.name: The White Rock, the second treachery
stops.campa: Higher up, elders come with branches and wreaths, offering guides and hostages. Hannibal trusts them exactly as far as their gorge: he puts the baggage and cavalry ahead and marches the heavy foot as rearguard, and when the guides spring the trap, boulders thundering down the couloirs, tribesmen on the slopes, the army is cut in two but not opened. All night Hannibal holds the bare white rock, the leukopetra the canon remembers, with half his force, apart from his horses and his baggage, until the column can reknit below. The mountains have now done their worst with men. What remains is the mountain itself.

stops.name: The summit of the pass, the snows and the sight of Italy
stops.campa: On the ninth day the army stands on the roof of the world as the Pleiades set: new snow falling on old, the dead of the climb behind them, the beasts gaunt. Two days he rests them on the summit. Which summit, Clapier or Traversette, the canon itself has argued ever since. Then he gathers the men on the lip of the pass and shows them, far below and blue with distance, the plains of the Po: Italy, laid open like a taken city. Eighteen centuries on, a German poet will slip over these mountains southward, hungry for that same light. Hannibal enters it with elephants.
stops.quote: You are climbing over the walls not of Italy only, but of Rome herself. The rest of the road is smooth and downhill; one battle, or at most two, will put the citadel and capital of Italy into your hands.
stops.quote_source: Livy 21.35, the speech on the summit
